name: All-Purpose Biscuits (Thanksgiving, Makes 12)
description: A plain, tall, flaky biscuit, doubled from our test batch so there are about 2 each for 5 adults. Made ahead and frozen, then baked straight from frozen. Adapted from All-Purpose Biscuits by Sam Sifton, NYT Cooking.
ingredients: 510 g all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
140 g cold unsalted butter, European style
steps: Cut the butter into thin pats and keep them in the fridge until needed. Line a sheet pan that fits in your freezer with parchment and flour your work surface well.
Sift the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt together, then tip them into a food processor.
Add the butter and pulse 5 or 6 times, just until the mix looks like coarse crumbs with pea-sized bits of butter still showing. If your processor is smaller than 11 cups, do this in two batches.
Put the mix in a large bowl, pour in the milk and stir with a fork only until it comes together in a shaggy ball.
Turn the dough onto the floured surface and pat it into a rectangle about 2.5 cm thick. Fold it in half and pat it flat again. Do this 3 times in all.
Cover loosely with a kitchen towel and let the dough rest for 30 minutes.
Pat the dough out to about 30 by 25 cm. Cut straight down with a floured biscuit cutter and lift it out without twisting, since twisting seals the edges and stops the rise.
Set the biscuits on the lined sheet pan and freeze for about 1 hour, until firm. Then move them to a gallon freezer bag.
Heat the oven to 425°F. Bake straight from frozen on a parchment-lined sheet pan for 13 to 20 minutes, until golden brown. Serve warm.
notes: Make ahead: steps 1 to 8 on Wednesday, about 1¼ hours including the rest and the freeze. Step 9 on Thursday, no thawing.

Swaps (only if needed; don't buy both): a floured drinking glass instead of a biscuit cutter (the edge is duller, so they rise a little less). A pastry cutter or two forks instead of the food processor.
Unbaked extras keep in the freezer for a month.
Nutrition: white flour and butter make these a holiday-only bake.
Source: adapted from All-Purpose Biscuits by Sam Sifton, NYT Cooking.
